warmup.q: A payments collection is sharded over three shards on { createdAt: 1 }, and the balancer has evened out the data: each shard holds about a third. At 09:00 card traffic starts, 3,000 inserts a second. How are those inserts spread?
options: About 1,000 a second on each shard, because the data is balanced
All 3,000 on one shard, the one that owns the chunk ending at MaxKey
mongos sends them round-robin, and the balancer moves them into place later
Evenly, because MongoDB hashes every shard key before it cuts chunks
warmup.why: Balance describes data already stored. Each chunk owns a range of createdAt, and every new payment is later than all the others, so every insert falls in the last range, the one that ends at MaxKey, and one shard owns it. The balancer can move old ranges away afterwards, but at 09:00 one primary takes all 3,000 writes. MongoDB hashes a key only when you shard with "hashed".

sections.h: One member: mongod, WiredTiger and the oplog
sections.html:
This case study puts four of the track's ideas into one product, MongoDB 9.0. Each shard is a single-leader replica set: a primary orders writes in a log, secondaries replay it, and an election replaces a dead primary (the Replication track's first lesson). The data is cut into key ranges or hash ranges (lesson 1). A tier of routers reads a map kept by a config service, and a balancer moves ranges by itself (lesson 3). And every index is local to its shard, so a query without the shard key asks them all (lesson 4). The Data models track ran a replica set; this lesson sets up the whole cluster. Start with one machine.

A MongoDB server is one process, mongod. It listens on port 27017 and keeps its data in files under --dbpath (/data/db in the lab containers). The code that lays documents out on disk is the storage engine, WiredTiger. It keeps each collection and each index as a B-tree (a sorted tree of pages; the Storage engines track's B+tree lesson builds one) in a file of its own, compressed with snappy. The pages you use stay in WiredTiger's cache, by default the larger of 50% of (RAM minus 1 GB) and 256 MB, so a 16 GB server gives it 7.5 GB. Every 60 seconds WiredTiger writes a checkpoint, a consistent snapshot of every file. Between checkpoints its journal, a write-ahead log that each change is appended to first, records every change, so a crash loses nothing the journal has.

One machine has the problem the Data models track ran into: when it dies, payments stop. So you keep copies, and MongoDB keeps them in step by copying operations: a logical log, in the Replication track's terms. Every write the primary applies is also recorded in the oplog, the collection local.oplog.rs. It's a capped collection: fixed in size, kept in insertion order, oldest entries dropped when it's full. Each entry describes one change, usually to one document. Secondaries pull new entries and apply them in the same order.

One rule makes the copying safe: every oplog entry is idempotent, so applying it twice gives the same result as applying it once. The primary therefore doesn't log what you asked for, $inc: { amountMinor: 100 }, but what came out of it, amountMinor: 4350. A secondary that crashes halfway through a batch applies the whole batch again, and ends in the same state. The Try-it shows the rewrite.

The oplog's size decides how long a member may be away. By default it's 5% of the free disk, at least 990 MB and at most 50 GB. The time between its oldest and newest entry is the oplog window. A secondary that returns within the window replays what it missed. One that was away longer has lost entries it needed and must copy every document again, an initial sync, which for 2 TB of payments can take most of a day. Do the sum for your write rate: at 2 GB of oplog an hour, a 50 GB oplog holds 25 hours. If a member can be down for a long weekend, raise the size with replSetResizeOplog or set a floor in hours with oplogMinRetentionHours.

Every MongoDB deployment is built from one part, the replica set: a primary orders writes in its oplog and secondaries replay it. A sharded cluster is several replica sets, each holding a slice of the data, plus one more replica set that holds the map of which slice lives where. The rest of the lesson builds that picture, one box at a time.

sections.h: Set up a replica set: members, priorities and elections
sections.html:
A replica set is set up in two steps. Start every member with the same set name, then tell one of them who the members are:

// each member was started with: mongod --replSet rs0 --bind_ip_all
rs.initiate({ _id: "rs0", members: [
  { _id: 0, host: "mongo1:27017", priority: 2 },
  { _id: 1, host: "mongo2:27017" },
  { _id: 2, host: "mongo3:27017" } ] })

env/mongo-rs.yml runs exactly this from mongo1's healthcheck. mongo1 stores the configuration, the others fetch it, and within seconds they elect a primary.

The election protocol, protocol version 1, is the failover from the Replication track made precise. It derives from Raft, which the Consensus track builds: members elect a leader by majority vote, and each election has a number, the term, so nobody votes twice in one term. Members send each other a heartbeat, a small "I'm alive" message, every 2 seconds. A secondary that hears nothing from the primary for electionTimeoutMillis, 10 seconds by default, becomes a candidate. It adds one to the term, votes for itself and asks the others. A member gives one vote per term, and only to a candidate whose oplog is at least as recent as its own. Votes from a majority of the voting members, 2 of 3, make a primary. The docs say the median election finishes within 12 seconds. A member with a higher priority calls elections sooner and, once it has caught up, takes the primary role back. Priority 0 means it never becomes primary.

Three member settings exist for special jobs:

  • hidden: true (with priority 0): drivers never send it reads. Use it for backups or a nightly report.
  • secondaryDelaySecs: 3600 (with hidden, priority 0 and votes: 0): applies the oplog an hour late. If a bad deploy runs deleteMany({}) on payments, this member still has them for an hour. The delay must be shorter than the oplog window.
  • arbiterOnly: true: votes, holds no data. Avoid it. With a primary, a secondary and an arbiter, losing the secondary leaves one copy, and w: "majority" writes (acknowledged once a majority of members have them) stall, because the only other voter can't store them. A third data-bearing member costs one more disk and is a real copy. Since 5.3 MongoDB refuses a second arbiter unless you set allowMultipleArbiters.

A set can have up to 50 members, at most 7 of them voting.

Reads have a setting too. Read preference picks the member that serves a read. The default, primary, sees every acknowledged write. secondary, secondaryPreferred and nearest spread reads out, but a secondary is behind by its replication lag: milliseconds normally, minutes during a long index build or a network problem. maxStalenessSeconds (90 at least) tells the driver to skip a secondary that has fallen further behind. Read a balance before a payment from the primary. A month-end statement can come from a secondary.

sections.h: Past one replica set: shards, config servers and mongos
sections.html:
A replica set puts every document on every member, and that gives it two ceilings. The data must fit one machine's disk, and the part you read must fit its cache: with 3 TB of payments and a 7.5 GB cache, most reads go to disk. And every write goes through one primary. If it takes 8,000 inserts a second at 70% CPU and Black Friday needs 25,000, more secondaries don't help, since each one replays all 25,000 writes too.

So split the collection over several replica sets. Build it up.

Version 1 splits in the application: accounts A-0000 to A-4999 on set 1, the rest on set 2, a rule in every service. It works until set 1 fills up. A third set means a new rule in every service at the same moment, and moving data while payments keep arriving.

Version 2 turns the rule into data: a table of key ranges and the set that holds each one. That table is now the most important data in the cluster, so it lives in a replica set of its own. And services shouldn't each read it: they talk to a router that reads it, keeps a copy in memory and forwards each operation. That's lesson 3's routing tier, and it's MongoDB's sharded cluster, in the figure:

  • A shard is a replica set (three members in production) holding part of each sharded collection.
  • The config server replica set holds the cluster's metadata in the config database: config.shards, config.collections, and config.chunks, which lists every range and its shard. It allows no arbiters and no delayed members. The balancer runs on its primary. If it can't elect a primary, the map is read-only: reads and writes go on, but nothing moves.
  • mongos is the router. It has no data and nothing on disk. Applications connect only to mongos, so run several, often one next to each application instance.

A sharded collection has a shard key, a field or fields in its documents, and its key space is cut into chunks (the 9.0 docs also call them ranges), each owned by one shard. For an insert, mongos computes the document's shard key, finds the chunk whose range holds it and sends the insert to that shard's primary. A query whose filter pins down the shard key is targeted: mongos asks only the shards that own matching chunks, and explain() says SINGLE_SHARD when that's one. A query without the shard key goes to every shard and mongos merges the answers, a scatter-gather read, SHARD_MERGE in explain(). It's lesson 4's local index at work: each shard indexes only its own documents, so nothing but the shard key tells mongos where to look. A scatter is as slow as the slowest shard and every shard pays for it, so more shards don't make it faster.

To build one: start shard members with mongod --shardsvr --replSet shard1, config members with mongod --configsvr --replSet cfg, initiate each set as in the previous section, start mongos --configdb cfg/cfg1:27017, and on mongos run sh.addShard("shard1/shard1:27017") for each shard. env/mongo-sharded.yml does all of that, with one member per set to fit your laptop. Since 6.0 you don't need sh.enableSharding() first: sh.shardCollection() creates what's missing.

sections.h: The shard key decides where inserts land and which reads scatter
sections.html:
mongos can only route by the shard key, so the key decides two things: which shard each insert goes to, and which reads are targeted. Judge a candidate by three properties first.

Cardinality is the number of distinct values. All documents with one value live in one chunk, so a key with 3 values can never use more than 3 shards. currency on EUR, USD and GBP payments is that key.

Frequency is how often the commonest value appears. Shard on merchantId, and M-0042, with a fifth of all payments, sits in one chunk that grows without limit. A chunk bigger than the chunk size that can't be split, because every document in it has the same shard key value, is a jumbo chunk. The lab makes one.

A monotonic key only grows: createdAt, a sequence number, or the ObjectId that MongoDB puts in _id when you don't, whose first 4 bytes are a timestamp. The last chunk's range ends at MaxKey, a special value above every other, and every new value is beyond all the existing ones, so every insert goes to that last chunk on one shard. The Try-it puts 20,000 ledger entries on shard1 and none on shard2.

Then choose how the key is cut. Ranged sharding cuts the values in their order: neighbours stay together, so a range of the key is targeted. Hashed sharding, { _id: "hashed" }, cuts the hash of the value instead. A growing key's inserts spread evenly, and an equality on the key is targeted, but a range is scattered, because neighbours hash far apart. A compound key with a hashed prefix mixes the two. Under { accountId: "hashed", createdAt: 1 } accounts spread evenly over the shards, and one account's payments sit together in time order, the way the Data models track's DynamoDB lesson built items with ACCT# and a time in the sort key.

Now test the candidates against the payments access patterns from the Data models track:

Shard key Inserts Account's newest payments Payment by id Merchant dashboard
{ createdAt: 1 } all on one shard scatter scatter scatter
{ merchantId: 1 } M-0042's shard is hot; jumbo chunk scatter scatter targeted
{ _id: "hashed" } even scatter targeted scatter
{ accountId: "hashed", createdAt: 1 } even targeted scatter scatter

For the payments core, take the last one. The account screen is the busiest read, and there are millions of accounts, each with a few payments a day. Give the merchant dashboard its own path, such as a reporting copy fed by a change stream (MongoDB's feed of committed changes, read from the oplog). Write the payment id lookup with the account id in the filter where you can.

One more rule follows from the key: MongoDB enforces a unique index across the cluster only if the shard key is its prefix, because each shard's index sees only its own documents. Even _id is unique only per shard when it isn't the shard key. So the idempotency key from the document-store lesson can't have a unique index on a collection sharded by account. Keep claims in a collection of their own, with the idempotency key as _id and as the shard key, as the Data models track did in DynamoDB.

sections.h: Chunks, the balancer, and changing the key later
sections.html:
A chunk is a range of shard key values owned by one shard, one document in config.chunks. The default chunk size is 128 MB. Before MongoDB 6.0.3, a shard split a chunk as soon as it grew past that size. Since 6.0.3 inserts never split anything (sh.status() still prints autosplit as enabled, and the autosplit commands do nothing). The balancer looks at data size instead. When the shard holding the most of a collection and the one holding the least differ by at least three chunk sizes (384 MB at the default), it moves a range, cutting about one chunk size off a bigger chunk as it goes. In the Try-it each range held 1,053 ledger entries, about 1 MB.

A migration keeps the range writable almost the whole time, and the stepper walks through one. The balancer sends moveRange to the donor shard. The recipient builds the indexes and copies the documents while the donor still takes the range's writes. The recipient then catches up on the changes made during the copy. The donor holds writes on the range briefly and commits the new owner to config.chunks. Later, when no open cursor needs them, the donor deletes its old copies. Until then they are orphans, and they still count in getShardDistribution(). A shard takes part in one migration at a time, so n shards run at most n/2 at once.

A jumbo chunk can't be split, and the balancer won't move a chunk that's too big. moveRange with forceJumbo: true can, but it blocks writes on the collection for the whole move. The cure is a better key. refineCollectionShardKey adds suffix fields to the existing key, which turns { merchantId: 1 } into { merchantId: 1, createdAt: 1 } so M-0042's chunk can split by time. reshardCollection (5.0 and later) builds the collection again under a new key: each recipient copies the documents it will own, builds indexes, replays the donors' oplog entries to catch up, and when less than 500 ms of work is left the donors block writes and the change commits. That needs room for a second copy, and time in proportion to the data. Plan it like a migration, because it is one.

MongoDB 8.0 added moves for whole collections, and 9.0 keeps them. An unsharded collection lives on one shard, at first the database's primary shard, so small collections pile up there. moveCollection moves one to another shard without sharding it. unshardCollection gathers a sharded collection back onto one shard, for one that turned out too small to need sharding. And reshardCollection to the same key is now a way to rebalance: every shard copies its new share at once, while the balancer moves one range per shard at a time. All three run on the resharding machinery, copy then catch up then cut over, and the Try-it shows its floor: at least reshardingMinimumOperationDurationMillis, 5 minutes by default, even for a tiny collection.

Zones pin key ranges to shards. With sh.addShardToZone("shard1", "EU") and a matching sh.updateZoneKeyRange, the balancer keeps EU accounts on EU hardware.

Before production, check:

  • three data-bearing members in every replica set, in three failure domains (racks or availability zones), and no arbiters;
  • w: "majority" (the default) for payments, and primary reads for decisions;
  • an oplog window longer than your longest planned outage, watched with rs.printReplicationInfo();
  • sharding only once one set can't hold the data or take the writes;
  • a shard key with many values, no dominant value and no steady growth, which your hottest queries include (analyzeShardKey, 7.0 and later, scores a candidate from sampled queries);
  • a three-member config server replica set, and several mongos near the applications;
  • unique indexes that start with the shard key;
  • a balancer window (activeWindow) if migrations hurt your peak hours.

analogy: Think of a payments archive that outgrew one building. It's split over several branch buildings, and each branch has a head clerk who files every new record in a day book and two assistants who copy it: a replica set. A central catalogue, kept in its own guarded office, lists which shelf ranges live in which branch: the config servers. Front desks in every office building look records up in a photocopy of the catalogue and send couriers to the right branch: mongos. At night a mover carts whole shelves from crowded branches to empty ones and updates the catalogue: the balancer. The analogy breaks in two places. MongoDB's mover works in daytime, while people keep adding records to the very shelf being moved, and that's why a migration copies first and catches up after. And a front desk's photocopy can be out of date, so a branch sometimes answers "not here any more" and the desk fetches a fresh copy, which is a StaleConfig error and a retry.
world: Your Quarkus payment service would connect to a list of mongos hosts, never to a shard, and the driver takes care of StaleConfig retries and of retryable writes after a failover. If you have used Oracle range partitioning by date, { createdAt: 1 } will feel familiar, but on Oracle every partition lives in one database, so a hot newest partition costs you nothing extra. In a sharded cluster the newest range sits on one machine, and that machine takes every insert. The shard key works like the key of a Kafka record: it decides the partition, and one busy key (a merchant on Black Friday) overloads one partition whatever the cluster's size. Give idempotency claims their own collection with the key as _id, as you would with a unique constraint in Oracle, because a unique index on a sharded collection must start with the shard key.
mistake: The most common mistake is sharding on what the busiest query filters by, usually time: { createdAt: 1 }, or the default ObjectId _id, which starts with a timestamp. It looks right in testing. Time-range queries are targeted, sh.status() shows balanced data, and the cluster runs fine at low traffic. In production every insert goes to the chunk that ends at MaxKey, one primary runs at 100% while the others idle, and the balancer spends its time moving yesterday's ranges off that shard. People make the choice because they read balance as the goal, when the goal is spread writes and targeted hot reads. The fix is a key whose leading part spreads writes, such as { accountId: "hashed", createdAt: 1 }, checked against the real access patterns (and with analyzeShardKey on sampled queries) before the first shard is added. Changing the key later is a reshardCollection: a full copy of the collection.

worked.title: Set up a sharded payments cluster, from processes to a checked shard key

steps.say: Start the processes. Three members for the config servers, three for each shard, and one mongos per application host. Every member of a set gets the same --replSet name.
steps.code: # config server replica set (on cfg1, cfg2, cfg3) mongod --configsvr --replSet cfg --port 27019 --bind_ip_all --dbpath /data/cfg # shard replica sets (on sh1a, sh1b, sh1c and sh2a, sh2b, sh2c) mongod --shardsvr --replSet shard1 --port 27018 --bind_ip_all --dbpath /data/db # routers, next to the payment service mongos --configdb cfg/cfg1:27019,cfg2:27019,cfg3:27019 --port 27017 --bind_ip_all

steps.say: Initiate each replica set from one of its members. Same shape for every shard; configsvr: true marks the config servers.
steps.code: // on cfg1 rs.initiate({ _id: "cfg", configsvr: true, members: [ { _id: 0, host: "cfg1:27019" }, { _id: 1, host: "cfg2:27019" }, { _id: 2, host: "cfg3:27019" } ] }) // on sh1a (and the same for shard2 on sh2a) rs.initiate({ _id: "shard1", members: [ { _id: 0, host: "sh1a:27018" }, { _id: 1, host: "sh1b:27018" }, { _id: 2, host: "sh1c:27018" } ] })

steps.say: On a mongos, add the shards, then shard payments on the key from the access patterns. On an empty collection MongoDB builds the shard key index itself and, for a hashed prefix, makes one chunk per shard.
steps.code: sh.addShard("shard1/sh1a:27018,sh1b:27018,sh1c:27018") sh.addShard("shard2/sh2a:27018,sh2b:27018,sh2c:27018") sh.shardCollection("sfz.payments", { accountId: "hashed", createdAt: 1 })

steps.say: Uniqueness that isn't the shard key gets a collection of its own. The idempotency key is the claim's _id and its shard key, so a duplicate fails on whichever shard owns it.
steps.code: sh.shardCollection("sfz.idempotency", { _id: "hashed" }) db.idempotency.insertOne({ _id: "idem-7f3a", paymentId: "pay-81723", expiresAt: new Date(Date.now() + 86400000) }) db.idempotency.createIndex({ expiresAt: 1 }, { expireAfterSeconds: 0 }) // a TTL index removes old claims

steps.say: Check the result before traffic arrives: the shards, the chunks, and that the account screen's query is targeted.
steps.code: sh.status() db.payments.getShardDistribution() db.payments.find({ accountId: "A-1001" }).sort({ createdAt: -1 }).limit(20).explain().queryPlanner.winningPlan.stage // SINGLE_SHARD: one account's payments live on one shard, in time order // optional: keep migrations out of the peak db.getSiblingDB("config").settings.updateOne({ _id: "balancer" }, { $set: { activeWindow: { start: "23:00", stop: "05:00" } } }, { upsert: true })

lab.title: Build a shard-key simulator: chunks, routing and the balancer
steps: Run the tests from the labs folder. No Docker needed. All ten fail with NotImplementedError.
Read ShardKeys.kt. Key (with MinKey and MaxKey), KeyRange, PaymentQuery and rangeFor are given. Write keyOf: four one-line keys, one per pattern. The first test passes.

In ShardedCluster.kt the constructor already shards an empty collection the way MongoDB 8.0 and later do: one chunk per shard for a hashed prefix, one chunk on the first shard for a ranged key. Write chunkFor and insert. The chunkFor and hashed-spread tests pass: 30,000 payments land between 9,500 and 10,500 per shard.
Write route. The targeting test passes: the same merchant dashboard query is SHARD_MERGE under { _id: "hashed" } and SINGLE_SHARD under { merchantId: "hashed", createdAt: 1 }.

Write splitLargeChunks, then balancerRound. The rest pass: 20 MB of time-ordered payments end at 8, 6 and 6 MB after 12 migrations, the next 1,000 inserts all hit the MaxKey chunk, and under { merchantId: "hashed" } M-0042 becomes a 4 MB jumbo chunk that never moves.

Experiment: in balancerRound, change the threshold from 3 chunk sizes to 1 and run the balancing test again. It moves more chunks and ends closer to even. That's the trade the docs describe: small differences tolerated in exchange for fewer migrations.
hints: chunks.floorEntry(key).value: the chunks cover MinKey to MaxKey with no gaps, so there is always one. Key is Comparable, so <= and > work on keys.
A chunk [min, max) overlaps the inclusive range [lo, hi] when min <= range.hi && max > range.lo.
Runs: walk chunk.keys.sorted() and start a new run whenever the key differs from the current run's first key.

Packing: if (current != null && (current.size + run.size).toLong() * docBytes <= chunkSizeBytes) current += run else pieces += ArrayList(run). Then remove the old chunk by its min and put each piece under its own min. Iterate over chunks.values.toList() so you don't change the map while walking it.

Pairing: sort once with compareByDescending<String> { bytes.getValue(it) }.thenBy { shards.indexOf(it) }, then walk inwards from both ends. chunks.values.firstOrNull { it.shard == from && !it.jumbo } is the donor's chunk with the smallest min, because a TreeMap iterates in key order.

drill.title: A replica set member list and a sharded collection, from memory
drill.prompt: Without looking, write the rs.initiate for a set rs0 where mongo1 is preferred as primary and mongo3 is a hidden, one-hour delayed copy that doesn't vote. Then write the commands, run on mongos, that add one shard shard1 (members sh1a, sh1b, sh1c on port 27018) and shard sfz.payments so that inserts spread and an account's newest payments are one targeted query. One line each: why no arbiter, and why not { createdAt: 1 }.

answer.html: rs.initiate({ _id: "rs0", members: [ { _id: 0, host: "mongo1:27017", priority: 2 }, // preferred primary { _id: 1, host: "mongo2:27017" }, { _id: 2, host: "mongo3:27017", priority: 0, hidden: true, // never primary, never read secondaryDelaySecs: 3600, votes: 0 } ] }) // an hour behind, no vote sh.addShard("shard1/sh1a:27018,sh1b:27018,sh1c:27018") sh.shardCollection("sfz.payments", { accountId: "hashed", createdAt: 1 }) // no arbiter: it holds no data, so losing one data member leaves a single copy // and w: "majority" writes stall; a third data-bearing member is a real copy // not { createdAt: 1 }: every insert is later than all others, so all of them // go to the chunk ending at MaxKey, on one shard

recap: A mongod stores collections and indexes as WiredTiger B-trees, with a cache of the larger of 50% of (RAM minus 1 GB) and 256 MB, checkpoints every 60 seconds and a journal between them.

Replication copies operations: the primary writes idempotent entries (results, not $incs) to the capped local.oplog.rs, and secondaries replay them. The oplog window is how long a member may be away without a full initial sync.

Elections follow a Raft-derived protocol: heartbeats every 2 s, a candidate after 10 s of silence, one vote per term, only for a candidate whose oplog is at least as recent. Priorities choose the preferred primary; hidden and delayed members do side jobs; arbiters are a false saving.

A sharded cluster is shards (replica sets), a config server replica set holding the chunk map and running the balancer, and stateless mongos routers. A filter with the shard key is targeted (SINGLE_SHARD); one without it scatters (SHARD_MERGE).

Pick a shard key with high cardinality, low frequency and no steady growth, that the busiest queries include. Monotonic keys put every insert on the MaxKey chunk; a dominant value makes a jumbo chunk; unique indexes must start with the shard key.

Since 6.0.3 inserts never split chunks. The balancer moves about one chunk size (128 MB default) at a time when shards differ by 3 chunk sizes, copying while writes continue. Fix a bad key with refineCollectionShardKey or a full reshardCollection; since 8.0, moveCollection and unshardCollection move whole collections.

explain.prompt: A teammate wants to shard the payments collection on { createdAt: 1 } because "every report filters by date, and sh.status() will show the data balanced". Explain what happens to inserts, what the balancer does about it, and which key you'd use instead.
explain.answer: A ranged key keeps values in order, and each chunk owns a range. Every new payment has a later createdAt than all the others, so every insert lands in the last chunk, the one that ends at MaxKey, and that chunk lives on one shard. That shard's primary takes 100% of the writes. The balancer only looks at stored data: when shards differ by three chunk sizes it moves old ranges off the full shard, so sh.status() does look balanced, but the newest range never leaves, and the hot shard stays hot. In the Try-it, after eight migrations the next 1,000 entries all still went to shard1. Date filters on reports are a weak reason anyway, because reports can scatter or run on a reporting copy. For the payments core I'd use { accountId: "hashed", createdAt: 1 }: the hash spreads the millions of accounts evenly, so inserts spread, and one account's payments stay together in time order, so the account screen, our busiest read, is a single-shard query. Idempotency claims go in their own collection keyed by the idempotency key, since a unique index must start with the shard key.

deeper.html:
The election details have one more dial. When a new primary is elected, it can spend up to catchUpTimeoutMillis copying newer writes that other reachable members have before it starts taking writes, which saves some w: 1 writes from rollback at the cost of a slower failover. The protocol versions page promises that pv1 preserves confirmed w: "majority" writes; anything less is a matter of luck and timing, as the rollback in the Data models track's document-store lesson showed. Zhou and Mu's NSDI 2021 paper describes the protocol as derived from Raft, with one big difference: secondaries pull the oplog from a sync source (which can be another secondary) instead of the primary pushing to every follower. That's why a set spread over two data centres can have the far secondaries copy from each other and send one stream across the link.

MongoDB 8.0 also added config shards: the config server replica set can store application data too, which saves a replica set in a small cluster (sh.isConfigShardEnabled() tells you). And since 7.0 analyzeShardKey scores a candidate key's cardinality, frequency and monotonicity from sampled queries. Run it before you shard.

Orphans matter for reads too. A shard still holding orphaned documents filters them out with a SHARDING_FILTER stage, which you saw at the top of each shard's plan in the Try-it's explain(). Reads at read concern available skip that filter and can return orphans, which is one more reason to leave read concern at its default for payments.

The AutoMerger joins adjacent chunks that sit on the same shard, so the chunk count doesn't grow forever as migrations cut ranges.
